pyqs.independentSolution: A=3.14×0.02²=0.001256 m²; μ=125×1×A=0.157 A m²; τ=μ×0.4×sin30°=0.0314 N m=314×10^-4. Angle is from axis, not plane. τ=0 for normal parallel B and maximal for perpendicular.

pyqs.independentSolution: One turn; A=0.001256 m². μ=100√2 A×A×(î+k̂)/√2=0.1256(î+k̂) A m². B=0.004(3î+2k̂) T. Cross product (î+k̂)×(3î+2k̂)=−2ĵ+3ĵ=ĵ, hence 0.0005024ĵ N m. Reversing current reverses torque.
pyqs.adaptation: Uses N m instead of the equivalent Wb A; states one turn and that the given unit normal follows the right-hand rule.

topics.title: Why does splitting a liquid drop need energy?
topics.question: A spherical liquid drop of diameter 2 mm breaks into 512 equal spherical droplets without losing liquid. If its surface tension is 0.08 N/m, what is the increase in surface energy, to the nearest microjoule?
topics.learningObjective: Conserve liquid volume to find new radii, then calculate the change in total surface area and count one or two interfaces correctly.

pyqs.independentSolution: R=0.001 m; 512r³=R³ gives r=R/8. Total final area=512×4πR²/64=8×4πR². ΔE=0.08×7×4π×10^-6=7.0336×10^-6 J. Positive; one drop N=1 gives zero; inverse coalescence reduces energy.
pyqs.adaptation: Original does not explicitly say equal droplets; equal spherical droplets and volume conservation are stated. Nearest microjoule matches the keyed option.

pyqs.independentSolution: Thin soap film has two interfaces. Radii 0.01 and 0.03 m; ΔA=8π(0.03²−0.01²)=0.0064π m². W=0.03×0.0064π=1.92π×10^-4 J. α is coefficient of π, not numerical energy in units of 10^-4 J.
pyqs.adaptation: Uses the paper’s coefficient of π exactly; explicitly treats the work as the reversible surface-energy increase at constant tension.

topics.title: How do you calculate crystal field energy in a tetrahedral complex?
topics.question: For high-spin tetrahedral metal ions with d², d⁴, d⁶ and d⁸ configurations, find the crystal field stabilisation energy of each in units of Δt. Include only the energy from orbital splitting.

pyqs.answer: d² −1.2Δt; d⁴ −0.4Δt; d⁶ −0.6Δt; d⁸ −0.8Δt (A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II)
pyqs.independentSolution: e orbitals lie at −0.6Δt and t₂ at +0.4Δt. High-spin occupancies e²t₂⁰,e²t₂²,e³t₂³,e⁴t₂⁴ give −1.2,−0.4,−0.6,−0.8. Barycentre check 2(−.6)+3(.4)=0; d5 and d10 splitting contributions zero. Pairing energy excluded.
pyqs.adaptation: Paraphrases matching table and states high-spin and splitting-only assumptions.

pyqs.answer: A, B and D true; C false
pyqs.independentSolution: e={dz²,dx²−y²} lower; t₂={dxy,dxz,dyz} higher. Thus A dxy=dxz>dx²−y² true; B dxy=dyz>dz² true; C dx²−y²>dz²>dxz false; D dx²−y²=dz²<dxz true.
pyqs.adaptation: Restates orbital comparisons in words to preserve accessible notation.

topics.title: How does rewriting a reaction change its equilibrium constant?
topics.question: At one temperature, 2XY ⇌ X₂ + Y₂ has K₁ = 2.5 × 10⁵, and XY + ½Z₂ ⇌ XYZ has K₂ = 5 × 10⁻³. All species are gases. Find K₃ for ½X₂ + ½Y₂ + ½Z₂ ⇌ XYZ, using the same equilibrium-constant convention throughout.
topics.learningObjective: Reverse, scale and add chemical equations while taking the reciprocal, power and product of their equilibrium constants.
topics.example: Follow the same A, B and C species through A ⇌ B and B ⇌ C, cancelling the intermediate B.
topics.description: Track what happens to K when an equation is reversed, multiplied by a number, or added to another reaction.
topics.alt: A to B and B to C combine to A to C; the intermediate B cancels and the two equilibrium constants multiply.
topics.scope: Chemistry Unit 6: law of chemical equilibrium and equilibrium constants Kp and Kc; Unit 4 relates standard Gibbs energy to K.
topics.difference: Prior lessons calculate equilibrium amounts/partial pressures or a Nernst reaction quotient. This changes the written reaction and transforms its equilibrium constant algebraically at fixed temperature.

pyqs.independentSolution: Reverse first and divide coefficients by 2: 1/2 X2+1/2 Y2⇌XY, K=K1^(-1/2). Add second reaction, cancel XY. K3=K2/√K1=.005/500=10^-5. Direct quotient multiplication cancels XY. All positive, same temperature and same K convention.
pyqs.adaptation: Capitalises the symbolic species; makes common temperature and consistent K convention explicit.

pyqs.independentSolution: New equation is one third of old: Knew=(2.7×10^-5)^(1/3)=(27×10^-6)^(1/3)=3×10^-2. Cubing result returns original K; not K/3.
pyqs.adaptation: Preserves paper’s formal symbolic species A₂, B₂ and C, explaining fractional coefficients as ratios.

topics.title: How do you turn a geometric progression into equations?
topics.question: The roots of x² − x + p = 0 are α and β, and the roots of x² − 4x + q = 0 are γ and δ. The numbers p and q are integers. If α, β, γ, δ form a geometric progression in that order, find |p + q|.
topics.learningObjective: Represent consecutive geometric-progression terms with a first term and a common ratio, convert given sums/products into equations, and check integer restrictions.
topics.example: Four successive terms u, ur, ur² and ur³ have pair sums related by r².
topics.description: Write consecutive terms as u, ur, ur² and ur³, then turn the given information into equations and check every restriction.
topics.alt: The pair u and ur becomes ur squared and ur cubed when both terms are multiplied by r squared.
topics.scope: Mathematics Unit 6: geometric and arithmetic progressions; Unit 2: relations between roots and coefficients.
topics.difference: Earlier AP lesson recovers terms from cumulative sums; earlier quadratic lesson tests sign. This represents a GP by repeated multiplication and converts root sums/products into constraints.

pyqs.independentSolution: Let roots u,ur,ur²,ur³. u(1+r)=1, ur²(1+r)=4 so r²=4; sum1 nonzero permits division. r=2 gives u=1/3,p=2/9, excluded by integer p. r=−2 gives u=−1; roots −1,2,−4,8; p=−2,q=−32; |p+q|=34. Verify roots in both quadratics.
pyqs.adaptation: Paraphrases while preserving order and both integer constraints.

pyqs.independentSolution: Let GP first term u, ratio r; AP first term r,difference u. GP: u(1+r)=8. AP sum10=5(2r+9u)=160, so r=16−9u/2. Hence 9u²−34u+16=0. u=(17±√145)/9, both valid, nonzero; requested sum34/9 by Vieta. Neither finite progression requires |r|<1.
pyqs.adaptation: Restates cross-identification of first term, ratio and difference explicitly.

topics.question: For the orbitals 2s, 3s, 3p and 4d, find the number of radial nodes and angular nodes in each.
topics.rationale: Two verified question IDs address a distinct prerequisite or misconception. Four official April papers inspected for today; cumulative nine-paper targeted corpus, without an exhaustive frequency or marks estimate.
topics.difference: Counts nodes of atomic orbitals from quantum numbers. Earlier lessons compare Bohr radii or occupy molecular antibonding orbitals.
topics.title: How do quantum numbers tell you the number of orbital nodes?
topics.learningObjective: Read n and l from an orbital label, count n−l−1 radial and l angular nodes, and distinguish angular nodes from nodal planes.
topics.example: Compare a radial spherical node with the angular nodal plane of a real p orbital.
topics.description: Separate radial nodes from angular nodes, then use n and l to count them without confusing every angular node with a plane.
topics.alt: A circular section represents a spherical radial node; a straight section represents the nodal plane separating two p-orbital lobes.
topics.scope: Chemistry Unit 2: quantum numbers and shapes of s, p and d orbitals.

pyqs.independentSolution: Use l=0,0,1,2 and radial n−l−1. Totals are n−1. Original A-IV B-III C-II D-I agrees with these counts, but says nodal planes for unspecified4d. Real dxy has two planes whereas dz² has two conical nodes.
pyqs.adaptation: Changes the original heading nodal planes to angular nodes and converts matching choices into counts. Explicitly discloses why unspecified4d does not imply two planes.

pyqs.locator: 5 April 2026 Shift 2, Q52 statement D, PDF pages 20–21
pyqs.answer: Statement D is false: 5d has two radial nodes. Counts for 5f,6s,4d,5p,5d are 1,5,1,3,2.
pyqs.independentSolution: n−l−1 gives 5−3−1=1,6−0−1=5,4−2−1=1,5−1−1=3,5−2−1=2. Full-key A and C only excludes D. Original A follows n+l tie rule, B incorrectly says same-subshell energy increases with Z, C compares sizes2px<3px.
pyqs.adaptation: Uses only statement D of the original multi-statement question, clearly labelled; does not claim the resulting short exercise is the full original.

topics.title: How do you find the time between two SHM positions?
topics.question: A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude A and period 5 s. Starting at x = A, how long does it take to reach x = A/√2 for the first time?
topics.learningObjective: Choose a phase from the starting position, convert its change to elapsed time, and recover angular frequency from a speed-displacement equation.
topics.example: A spring-mounted block starts at its rightmost position and moves towards the centre.
topics.description: Use the starting position to choose a cosine, then turn the phase change into a fraction of one period.
topics.alt: A block at a spring’s rightmost position corresponds to phase zero; a quarter cycle later it reaches the centre.
topics.scope: Physics Unit 10: simple harmonic motion, displacement as a function of time, phase and time period.
topics.difference: No earlier article teaches SHM phase or elapsed time. It is distinct from electromagnetic-wave field direction and force interaction pairs.

pyqs.independentSolution: x=A cos(2πt/T) from right extreme. First arrival gives cosθ=1/√2, θ=π/4, t=T/8=5/8 s. A cancels; t<T/4 as required.
pyqs.adaptation: Makes the first arrival explicit; preserves the original amplitude and period.

pyqs.answer: T = 2π s; keyed coefficient 44 corresponds to π ≈ 22/7
pyqs.independentSolution: In SI units v²=50−x² matches ω²(A²−x²), so ω=1 rad/s, A=√50 m and T=2π s. Original T=X/7 gives exact X=14π≈43.9823 and keyed integer44; do not present 44/7 as exact.
pyqs.adaptation: Asks for the exact period, states SI units, renames the paper’s repeated x coefficient X, and explains the integer-key approximation.

topics.title: Does an absolute value always make a sharp corner?
topics.question: Let f(x) = e^(sin |x|) − |x| for all real x. Is f differentiable everywhere, and is it increasing on (−π, −π/2)?
topics.learningObjective: Locate possible joins, simplify even outer functions, and compare one-sided slopes before deciding whether an absolute value or maximum causes nondifferentiability.
topics.example: Compare the slopes of y=|x| and y=x² at their common joining point x=0.
topics.description: Compare the left and right slopes at each possible join. A modulus is a place to check, rather than proof of a corner.
topics.alt: The graph of absolute x has slopes minus one and plus one at zero, while x squared has slope zero from both sides.
topics.scope: Mathematics Unit 7: continuity, differentiability, composite functions and monotonicity.
topics.difference: The earlier quadratic article tests global sign; this checks local slopes where formulas meet, including cancellation of corners.

pyqs.answer: Both statements are true. f′(0)=0 and f′(x)>0 on (−π,−π/2).
pyqs.independentSolution: For x>0 derivative e^(sin x)cosx−1 tends0; x<0 derivative1−e^(−sin x)cosx tends0. Direct difference quotient at0 also tends0, using (e^(sin t)−1)/t→1. Elsewhere smooth. For −π<x<−π/2, cosx<0 so1−e^(−sin x)cosx>0.
pyqs.adaptation: Paraphrases the two statements without changing the function or interval.

pyqs.independentSolution: cos|u|=cosu makes x=±1/2 smooth. Branches6x and2+3x² cross at1±1/√3; slopes6 versus6x differ there. |x−1|cos(x²−1/4) is smooth at those crossings. At1 max selects6x locally and derivative jump of other term is2cos(3/4)≠0. All three lie in (−π,π).
pyqs.adaptation: Writes max(6x,2+3x²) in words to avoid notation ambiguity; preserves cosine applied to absolute x²−1/4 and the open domain.
